today.h: Buy Everything but AI: a Bond Rally, a Rotation — and a Late Rebound
today.c1: The rescue bid: a day after the AI complex's worst session since July, the selloff went global — South Korea's Kospi fell 7.6% — before Wall Street's dip buyers answered. The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to 7,744.06, halting a three-day drop; the Dow jumped 556 points (+1.08%) to 52,177.69 behind Nike, Salesforce and Home Depot as investors rotated out of tech; the Nasdaq erased a ~1.4% intraday loss to close +0.08% at 26,713.03. An equal-weighted version of the S&P climbed 1.4% — more than four times the benchmark — and eight of 11 sectors closed green (health care +1.9% best; energy -1.6% worst). The mechanics: hot prints — PPI +6.3% y/y, the highest annual rate since December 2022, and retail sales that doubled estimates — did not re-arm the rate trade: October hike odds fell to ~29% (December ~88%), the 10Y dropped 10bp to 5.09%, and the dollar slid 0.5% to ~102.0. The AI file stayed the swing factor: CoreWeave — whose credit-risk gauge hit a record — reversed a 9.5% morning loss to close +5.9% after Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended it; Nvidia itself fell 1.8% as the S&P's heaviest weight, and TSMC slid ~1.8% despite record profits. Oil split: WTI +3.0% to $97.97 on an 8.6M-barrel EIA draw and fresh Hormuz attacks; Brent held $105.92 (-0.1%). Gold rose 1.5% to a $4,169.7 December settle; bitcoin briefly broke $80,000 before recovering to ~$82.1k. Next: Warsh speaks tonight in Bangkok; Friday brings import prices and industrial production.
today.c4:
• The rotation is the trade to watch: money left chips for bonds, defensives and small caps — if breadth keeps carrying the index while the AI complex earns its way back, the scare stays contained.
  • The credit file is the new rate axis: CoreWeave's gauge at a record, ~$50B of debt and default insurance near 1,000bp — AI funding costs are now the market's most-watched number, and Huang's defense bought time, not a fix.
  • Warsh tonight is the gate: CPI and PPI ran hot yet October odds fell to ~29% — the market is betting the Fed won't add to the wobble; a hawkish surprise is the risk into the Oct 27-28 meeting.

chains.t: ① The Rescue Bid: a Bond Rally Meets the AI Scare — and Everything Else Gets Bid
steps: The overnight leg: Wednesday's AI selloff went global — Asia's chip markets cratered and the S&P opened ~0.6% lower; the Nasdaq's early hole reached ~1.4%
The flood: bonds took the flows — the 10Y fell 10bp to 5.09%, the dollar slid 0.5% to ~102.0, and gold rose 1.5% to a $4,169.7 December settle
The rotation bid: an equal-weighted S&P 500 climbed 1.4% — more than four times the cap-weighted index; the Dow jumped 556 points (+1.1%); small caps rose 1.4%; 8 of 11 sectors closed green
The rescue: Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended CoreWeave's financial health; the stock flipped from a 9.5% morning loss to close +5.9%; the Nasdaq erased its 1.4% loss to finish +0.1%
The scoreboard: S&P +0.33% to 7,744.06, Dow +1.08%, Nasdaq +0.08% — a breadth day, not a tech day
chains.d: The main chain: the AI scare's follow-through met a wall of rotation money — bonds, defensives and small caps took the flows, and a late rescue steadied the complex itself.

news.fact: Wall Street staged a comeback after losses driven by concerns about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence trade. The S&P 500 halted a three-day drop as Nvidia Corp.'s chief Jensen Huang defended the financial health of AI computing supplier CoreWeave Inc., a major customer in which the company is also an investor. In a sign of rotation to other sectors, an equal-weighted version of the S&P 500 climbed 1.4%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 1.1%, or 550 points, behind gains from the likes of Nike, Salesforce, and Home Depot. The benchmark S&P 500 rose 0.3%, while the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite erased steep losses to finish up 0.1%.

The S&P 500 advanced 0.3%, recovering from an early decline of approximately 0.6%. The Nasdaq Composite finished 0.1% higher after reversing an intraday loss of approximately 1.4%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell approximately 10 basis points to 5.09%.

All told, the S&P 500 rose 25.12 points to 7,744.06. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556.21 to 52,177.69, and the Nasdaq composite added 20.16 to 26,713.03. CoreWeave fell as much as 9.5% in the morning after tumbling 15.5% a day earlier; it later flipped to a gain and finished 5.9% higher. The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 5.09% from 5.19% late Wednesday.
The U.S. dollar index declined 0.5% to 102.04.
Spot gold was trading near $4,168.70 an ounce, up $64.20, or 1.56%, while spot silver was trading near $57.310, up $1.800, or 3.24%.

chains.t: ② The AI File: a Record Credit Gauge, Korea's Crash — and the Bailout Question
steps: Korea cratered: the Kospi fell 7.6% — its worst day since July, now 39% below June's record — and Japan's Nikkei lost 4.9%
The credit file: CoreWeave's credit-risk gauge hit an all-time high; its default insurance near 1,000bp implies a ~63% five-year default chance, up from ~30% a year ago, against ~$50B of debt (LSEG)

The US echo: Dell and HPE ranked among the S&P 500's worst performers for a second straight day; Seagate (-3.2%) and Western Digital (-2.1%) weighed on the Roundhill DRAM ETF (-1.5% after Wednesday's 5% slide)
TSMC's paradox: a record sixth straight quarter of profits and strong Q4 guidance — yet its US-listed shares fell as much as 5.3% before closing -1.8%

The debate: 'Is demand for AI real? Yes... but that does not mean every company building the infrastructure will generate attractive returns' (Crossbridge's Manish Singh); 'AI may be the future. Debt servicing is still the present.'
The heaviest weight: Nvidia -1.8% — the largest single drag on the S&P 500 — though it more than halved a 3.8% morning loss
chains.d: The AI file: the credit gauge at a record and Korea's crash set the morning tone — but chips stopped falling before the close.

news.fact: South Korea's Kospi index — dominated by two chip companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix — fell to its worst day since July. It has dropped 39% since setting a record in June. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 4.9%.

A measure of credit risk at the data-center operator hit an all-time high, triggering fresh jitters about the AI sector. 'Two questions matter. Is demand for AI real? Yes,' said Manish Singh at Crossbridge Capital. 'The structural opportunity is real, but that does not mean every company building the infrastructure will generate attractive returns for investors... AI may be the future. Debt servicing is still the present.'

CoreWeave has about $50 bln in debt, and the cost of insuring it against default has risen to around 1,000 basis points, implying a nearly 63% chance of default in five years, up from about 30% a year ago, according to LSEG data.

Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise ranked among the worst performers in the S&P 500 for a second straight day. Seagate Technology and Western Digital weighed on Roundhill's Memory ETF (DRAM), which was down about 1.5% following a 5% drop yesterday.

Nvidia fell 1.8% and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. TSMC's stock dropped as much as 5.3% in the morning before finishing with a more modest loss of 1.8%; the bellwether for the AI industry reported a profit that topped analysts' high expectations and said it expects strong demand to continue in the final three months of 2026.

chains.t: ③ The Barrel's Two-Sided Day: Relief Talk vs a Sunk Ship — WTI +3%, Brent Flat
steps: The morning dip: Washington floated easing sanctions on the 'shadow fleet' of tankers and the IEA agreed to accelerate releases — crude slid early before buyers returned

The escalation: a Singapore-registered container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by a projectile (its 21 crew evacuated safely; a second vessel was damaged) — and Iran said it is 'counting the moments' until it can strike US warships
The draw: EIA crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels last week — versus a 288,000-barrel draw expected — and the Houthis fired on Aden's presidential palace, killing two guards
The settles: WTI +$2.88 (+3.0%) to $97.97; Brent -14 cents (-0.1%) to $105.92 — the benchmark spread narrowed to ~$8
The divergence: energy closed worst among sectors (-1.6%) even as crude settled higher — Saudi crude kept flowing through alternative routes and the release headlines weighed on the group
chains.d: The barrel's two-sided day: policy supply met war supply — WTI won on the draw, Brent sat still, and energy equities never joined the rally.

news.fact: Brent crude was little changed on Thursday as investors weighed possible US steps to ease restrictions on the world's 'shadow fleet' of tankers, while conflict in the Middle East kept a geopolitical risk premium in the market. The international benchmark settled down 14 cents, or 0.13%, at $105.92 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled up $2.88, or 3.03%, to $97.97 a barrel, after a large US crude stock draw helped support prices.
Crude inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 288,000-barrel draw.

The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire; the ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated. A second vessel, the GFS Giselle, was also hit and sustained damage to its hull. 'Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law,' the Singapore maritime authority said.

The International Energy Agency agreed to release over 20 million barrels of diesel to the market as soon as possible and any oil remaining from a record emergency reserves release pledged in March; Spain will release 4.4 million barrels from strategic reserves in October.

U.S. crude oil prices rose as traders assessed potential supply disruptions following attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz; WTI for November gained about 3%, or $2.88, to close at $97.97 per barrel, while Brent for December fell 14 cents to settle at $105.92.

chains.t: ④ Hot Data, Softer Pricing: the PPI Paradox
steps: The print: PPI +1.3% m/m and +6.3% y/y — the fastest monthly jump since March 2022 — with energy +10.8% and gasoline +20.3%; retail sales doubled estimates at +0.8%; claims 199,000
The puzzle: a second hot inflation print in two days, yet October hike odds fell to ~29% (from ~37%) and December held ~88% — the market priced a Fed that won't add to the wobble
The Fed voices: San Francisco's Mary Daly and supervision chief Michelle Bowman underscored that an immediate rate hike might not be required, tempering expectations

The read: 'Neither the CPI nor PPI show inflation moving back towards the Fed's target... the retail sales report wasn't soft enough to shift the Fed's focus away from inflation' (Fifth Third's Bill Adams)
The gates: Warsh speaks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok tonight (11:30 p.m. ET); Friday brings import/export prices and industrial production; the pre-meeting blackout starts Saturday
chains.d: The data ran hot; the pricing ran cold — the market is betting the Fed won't stack a rate shock on top of the AI wobble.

news.fact: Wholesale prices rose 1.3% month-over-month and 6.3% year-over-year, up from a respective 0.4% and 5.4% in August and ahead of economists' expectations of 0.6% and 5.5%. September U.S. retail sales doubled estimates with a 0.8% rise, and weekly jobless claims came in a tick below expectations at 199,000. According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29% likelihood the Fed will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks and an 88% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point in December.

San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman underscored that an immediate rate hike might not be required, tempering expectations of an October rate hike. Traders are now pricing in about a 30% chance of a rate hike later this month, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.

'On balance, we think Warsh will talk in a way that does not suggest an October hike,' said Krishna Guha at Evercore. 'Warsh will be mindful of the global wobble in tech stocks and signs financing conditions are tightening for more exposed AI names, on top of the prior move up in longer-term yields.' The Fed chief is due to speak late Thursday New York time in Bangkok.

'Neither the CPI nor PPI show inflation moving back towards the Fed's target, leaving the Fed with "more work to do," in Chair Warsh's words at Jackson Hole earlier this year,' said Bill Adams, Chief U.S. Economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank. 'The retail sales report wasn't soft enough to shift the Fed's focus away from inflation.'

chains.t: ⑤ The Rotation's Receipts: Consumers Bid, Health Care Leads — and the Breadth Test
steps: The Dow's engine: Nike +5.2% — a stock down ~45% for the year heading into the session — plus Salesforce +4.6% and Home Depot +4.3% helped power the 556-point advance
The consumer bid: Walmart +1.5% on a Deutsche Bank upgrade, Sherwin-Williams +3.8% and McDonald's +1.8% rose as investors rotated into 'more defensive consumer-centric stocks'
The health bid: health care +1.9%, the best of 11 sectors — Moderna +4.5%, Veeva +5.3%, Eli Lilly +3.5%, UnitedHealth +2.8%, Amgen +1.9%
The one-offs: International Paper +6.9% on talks to sell its EMEA packaging unit; Marsh & McLennan +4.6% on a stronger profit
The counterweights: Rocket Lab -6.6% after delaying its Neutron debut to next year; bitcoin briefly broke below $80,000 before recovering
chains.d: The rotation's receipts: the money that left chips went shopping — consumers, health care and small caps got paid, and the losers were mostly the AI complex and the delayed.

news.fact: Shares of sportswear giant Nike, which were down 45% for the year heading into Thursday's session, jumped 6% Thursday afternoon to lead gains on the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Sherwin-Williams, Home Depot, Walmart, and McDonald's also climbed, helping lift the index 1%, while AI darlings Nvidia and Amazon declined.

The S&P 500 Health Care Sector is up roughly 2.5% Thursday afternoon to help the benchmark index eke out a fractional gain, with Moderna, Veeva Systems and Eli Lilly and Co. leading the sector; UnitedHealth Group and Amgen were each up more than 3%.

Walmart shares were up 2% to around $119 in recent trading, among the biggest gainers in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, after Deutsche Bank lifted its rating to 'buy' and its target to $136 from $113.

Shares of International Paper are soaring 7% to rank among the top S&P 500 gainers Thursday after the firm said that it is 'evaluating unsolicited inbound inquiries in relation to its EMEA Packaging Business, and is in discussion with potential bidders.'

Rocket Lab stock is sinking sharply after the aerospace company pushed back the launch of its Neutron rocket to next year; shares were down 11% in recent trading and are nearly 70% off their May record. Bitcoin briefly sank below the $80,000 level — the lowest since mid-September — after a pair of key inflation readings raised rate-hike expectations.

Marsh & McLennan helped lead the way and rallied 4.6% after the insurance and professional services firm that updated its brand name to Marsh reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.

mtd.h: October, Eleven Sessions In: Three Repricings Landed — the Rotation Answered
mtd.d: S&P 7,651.5 to 7,744.06 (+1.21% MTD): eleven sessions delivered two record closes, a 2002-ceiling re-test — and three repricings whose latest beat met a rotation bid.
mtd.c1: Eleven sessions into October and the month's arc is complete: two record closes (the first above 7,800), the 2002 ceiling re-tested at 24-year highs, and three repricings — wireless (10/9), the AI complex (10/12-13), and the inflation reckoning (10/14-15) — whose latest beat met a broad rotation bid. The S&P is +1.21% MTD at 7,744.06; the Nasdaq -0.55%; the Dow +2.50%. The fuel: AI compounding and a live deal tape. The tax: hot prints (CPI 3.7% y/y, PPI 6.3% y/y) that nonetheless left October hike odds at ~29% by the window's end; a 10Y that touched a 24-year high of 5.36% then closed 5.09% (-20bp MTD); Brent +8.1% on the December basis. Beneath: Energy (+8.2%), Staples (+7.5%) and Utilities (+5.6%) lead sectors, while Tech (-3.4%) sits at the bottom of the pack. Gates: the Oct 27-28 meeting — with Warsh speaking tonight.
mtd.c4:
• October's verdict so far: the records came early, three repricings followed — and the third met buyers, not capitulation; the month's engine (AI, deals) keeps running while the rate axis charges rent.
  • The dispersion signature holds: the barrel's beneficiaries and defensives lead; the AI complex's crowded corners get taxed — most recently by CPI and PPI.
  • The month's referee is still the Fed: odds fell to ~29% despite hot prints, and the Oct 27-28 meeting decides whether the repricing gets another round.

chains.t: ① Eleven Sessions, One Arc: the Records, the Ceiling — and the Repricings
steps: The opening stretch: records — the first close above 7,800 and a Nasdaq record — even as the 10Y pushed toward 24-year highs
Mid-window: the 2002 ceiling re-tested at 24-year highs — each re-test still bought at auction
The repricings: wireless (10/9); the AI complex's global unwind (10/12-13); then the inflation reckoning (10/14-15) — hot prints that didn't re-arm hike odds (October ends the window at ~29%)
The flows: the third repricing's worst beat met a rotation bid — bonds bid, the 10Y closing the window at 5.09% (-20bp)
The month's math: S&P +1.21%, Nasdaq -0.55%, Dow +2.50% — dispersion, not direction
chains.d: Eleven sessions in: records early, a ceiling re-tested — then three repricings, the last met by buyers. October's engine keeps running; the rate axis keeps charging rent.

news.fact: According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 37% likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, up from 22% before the reading, and a 91% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting, up from 88% before the data.

According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29% likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks and an 88% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.

Stocks surged Friday, pushing the major indexes to weekly gains, as tech shares rebounded from the previous session's sell-off. The 10-year Treasury yield ended the week around 5.24%, two days after it briefly neared 5.37%, its highest level in more than 24 years.

chains.t: ② The Month's Split: Inflation Beneficiaries Lead — and the AI Complex's Count
steps: Sector map: Energy (+8.2%), Staples (+7.5%) and Utilities (+5.6%) lead; Tech (-3.4%) sits at the bottom of the pack
Breadth warning: Goldman Sachs flags the narrowest participation since the dotcom bubble, with the median stock nearly 20% off its highs
Loser map: memory, equipment and neocloud names led every down-leg this month
The new wrinkle: the third repricing's worst beat met a rotation bid — consumers and health care got paid as tech bled
The signature: dispersion, not direction — a ~12-point spread between the month's best and worst sectors
chains.d: October's template: own the barrel's beneficiaries and the defensives; the repricings keep re-cutting the AI complex's crowded corners.

news.fact: Shares of the country's largest telecommunications giants are slumping amid worries about growing competition from SpaceX.

Memory makers Micron and SK Hynix saw their stocks fall after Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced significant progress on a new memory-cell design aimed at increasing storage density; CXMT aims to introduce a new server memory product built on the architecture by the end of 2026.
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index dropped 4.3%, down for a sixth straight session, its longest losing streak since May 2025.

chains.t: ③ The Barrel, Week Two: Re-Armed Above $100 — Then Two-Sided
steps: The bid stack: the heaviest tanker-attack week of the war, strike-risk headlines and Isaias shut-ins re-armed the war premium above $100
Policy answered twice: the IEA's accelerated release — and the Russia diesel deal (now downplayed by its author)
Week two's new layers: escalation kept coming — another round of the same fight
The numbers: Brent from ~$98 (Dec basis) to $105.92 (+8.1% MTD); WTI +8.4% to $97.97
The band: $100-107, with spikes sold and dips bought all month
chains.d: The barrel's second week: supply shocks met policy supply — and the market bought both sides of the $100-107 band.

news.fact: Approximately 62.9% of daily offshore oil production, or 1.28 million barrels per day, has been shut in as Hurricane Isaias strengthens ahead of an expected landfall.

Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began — cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
'Constraints on the diesel market will extend well into next year,' the International Energy Agency warned, with gasoil supply falling short of demand in 4Q26.

Brent crude settled down 14 cents, or 0.13%, at $105.92 a barrel; US West Texas Intermediate crude futures settled up $2.88, or 3.03%, to $97.97, after a large US crude stock draw helped support prices.

qtd.h: Q4's First Eleven Sessions: +1.21% — Records, a Ceiling, and the Reckonings
qtd.d: 9/30 7,651.5 to 10/15 7,744.06 (+1.21% QTD): the quarter's opening stretch delivered two record closes, a 10Y round trip from 5.29% to 24-year highs and back, and three repricings — the last met by a rotation bid.
qtd.c1: Q4 is eleven sessions old and the template is set: the S&P +1.21% QTD at 7,744.06 (its first close above 7,800 came in week one), the Nasdaq -0.55%, the Dow +2.50%. The quarter's themes: a live deal tape, AI compounding — one revenue scare, answered — a long end that did both (fresh 24-year highs, then a pullback), and an inflation reckoning that ended with October hike odds at ~29%, not higher. Dispersion is the character: Energy (+8.2%), Staples (+7.5%) and Utilities (+5.6%) lead while Tech (-3.4%) has slid to the bottom; Brent +8.1% (December basis); gold -0.4%; the dollar +0.5%. Gates ahead: the Oct 27-28 meeting, earnings season — and Warsh tonight.
qtd.c4:
• Q4's opening trade: 'no October hike' got cheaper to hold, not dearer — the market faded two hot prints; the Fed's reaction function is now the whole game.
  • The dispersion signature: the barrel's beneficiaries and defensives get paid; the AI complex's crowded corners get taxed — then rescued.
  • Duration: the 10Y still caps multiples — but its retreat to 5.09% was the rotation's enabler; a quiet bond market remains the bull case's first draft.

Policy supplied: the IEA's accelerated release — and the Russia diesel deal
Both met in a $100-107 band: spikes sold, dips bought

ytd.h: The Bull Meets the Referee: S&P +13.13% as the 10Y's +93bp Sets the Terms
ytd.d: S&P +13.13%, Nasdaq +14.93%, Dow +8.56% with eleven sessions of Q4 logged — AI and earnings carry; the 10Y's +93bp, a hot CPI-PPI pair and an eighth month of war tax the rest.
ytd.c1: The year's base case holds — with the same referee: the bull runs on AI capex and earnings, fighting two taxes — a 10Y up 93bp to 5.09% (fresh 24-year highs printed this month) and oil up ~71% as the war grinds through its eighth month — plus the year's newest twist: hot September prints (CPI 3.7%, PPI 6.3%) that the market increasingly expects the Fed to answer cautiously (October odds ~29%). The scoreboard: S&P +13.13%, Nasdaq +14.93%, Dow +8.56%; underneath, Energy (+48.9%) leads the year while Consumer Discretionary (-5.0%) lags; Comms (-4.5%) and Utilities (-2.4%) also lag. Nvidia +16.5% YTD as the AI complex's repricings (memory, equipment, credit) now cut both ways. Gold -3.9% as real rates, not war, dominated; December prices ~88%.
ytd.c4:
• The year's lesson holds: buy where earnings compound (AI infrastructure), rent where rates rule — and the credit file is the newest rent collector.
  • Rates: the 10Y's +93bp is 2026's biggest tax — its October retreat is the bull's best friend; a confirmed Fed pause remains the largest single bullish catalyst left.
  • The bull turned four (10/12) with the AI trade's fault lines visible: power, credit, competition — and now rate sensitivity.

chains.t: ① The Bull Market Continues — With a Referee
steps: The scoreboard: S&P +13.13%, Nasdaq +14.93%, Dow +8.56% — two record closes added in October; the bull turned four on 10/12
The engine: AI capex and earnings — Nvidia +16.5% YTD ($217.23); TSMC posted a record sixth straight quarter of profits
The character: record runs met with ceiling re-tests, not breaks — buyable dips (until this week's inflation prints)
The breadth: Energy (+48.9%) leads the year; Consumer Discretionary (-5.0%) now lags
chains.d: The bull holds — four years old — as AI and earnings carry the year; the 10Y, the war and now CPI-PPI tax the rest.

news.fact: Chipmakers, which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers on the day, falling 3.4%.

The bull market turned four on Monday, with many strategists expecting more room for stocks to run. However, concerns over an AI bubble, elevated Treasury yields, and geopolitical uncertainty present hurdles.

steps: The rates tax: 10Y 4.16% to 5.09% (+93bp), 30Y +59bp — fresh 24-year highs printed into October
The Fed answered: a September hike (first since July 2023); December prices ~88%, October ~29% after two hot prints the market faded
The barrel: WTI +70.6% YTD as the war tightened crude — and CPI's gasoline +34.2% y/y is the pass-through; pump prices $4.33/gal vs $3.08 a year ago
The toll: gold -3.9%, rate-sensitives lag, multiples capped
chains.d: 2026's second inflation wave: the Fed re-hiked, the 10Y paid +93bp — and this week showed the CPI-PPI channel is still live.

news.fact: Tight global crude supplies during the Iran war have sent US crude soaring more than 60% so far this year, stoking inflation pressures. In response to those pressures, the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time since July 2023.
Consumers pay $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, compared to about $3.08 per gallon a year earlier, according to AAA.
'Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates,' said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.

chains.t: ③ The AI Platform — and Its First Real Stress Test
steps: The platform: AI capex compounding — TSMC's record quarter; Anthropic's Q3 revenue at $16.8B ahead of a planned listing
The buildout moved onto credit: SpaceX's $40B raise; Broadcom's $50B for OpenAI; CoreWeave's ~$50B of debt — its credit-risk gauge now at a record
The first revenue question (FT, 10/8) — answered within a day (Bloomberg, 10/9)
The stress test: a global memory repricing (CXMT), a rate shock (CPI), and a credit gauge at a record — met by a rotation bid
chains.d: The AI trade's year: capex compounding, funded on credit — a revenue question answered, then a competition-and-rate stress test.

news.fact: A little over a week after it was reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue was approaching $70 billion, the AI lab is said to have told investors the real figure is some $20 billion lower — 'approaching $50 billion.'
Bloomberg reported that OpenAI expects to reach or exceed $70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of the year, helping quell worries that the AI boom is running out of steam.

Selling has been particularly intense in CoreWeave, which has issued $22 billion of bonds and $26 billion of loans, according to LSEG data. A CoreWeave bond that was issued in June yielding 9.625% recently yielded 15%.

steps: The war's eighth month: crude 'soaring more than 60%' YTD — supply risk as the year's background hum
The month's escalation: the heaviest tanker-attack week; 24 ships hit in the two weeks to 10/11; a container ship sank in Hormuz
The storm layer: Isaias shut-ins — 62.9% of Gulf output at the peak
The policy stack: G7/IEA releases (20M+ barrels of diesel agreed this week) — and the Russia diesel deal
chains.d: War as the norm: the barrel carries the premium — and policy carries the offsets.

news.fact: Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began — cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October; of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
Approximately 62.9% of daily offshore oil production, or 1.28 million barrels per day, has been shut in as Hurricane Isaias strengthens.

steps: From cuts to hikes: a September hike (first since July 2023)
The odds: October ~29%, December ~88% (CME FedWatch) — two hot prints faded
The dollar +3.8% as the regime re-priced; gold -3.9% as real rates dominated
The gates: the Oct 27-28 meeting — Warsh speaks tonight; every print still moves the whole curve
chains.d: The regime changed in 2026: cuts became hikes, the dollar firmed — and this week showed the market can still fade the prints.

news.fact: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, but the timing of those hikes is 'flexible.'

According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29% likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, and an 88% likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.
